blocks.text: VII. He (in his Sacred Miscellanies, book 6, ch. 11) understands both דביונים and חריונים (the former of which is written in the margin, the latter in the text) as the crop of doves, [II, 578] their belly and entrails. As if they were called דביונים, that is, the flux of doves, because those who cut up and gut doves let these flow out, or slip down to the ground. And חריונים, that is, κοιλία [koilia], or the belly of doves. For he tries to prove that חריונים are the belly and entrails of doves as follows: "The Hebrew חור first means white; 2. a hole, from the brightness of the light that is usually seen through it; 3. τρώγλην [trōglēn] a cavity, which is a kind of hole; 4. the belly, in Greek κοιλίαν [koilian], which is a notable cavity of the human body; whence alvus [belly] is named as if alveus [hollow], κοιλία ἀπὸ τοῦ κοίλου [koilia apo tou koilou]; 5. the excrement enclosed in the belly, by a metonymy of the contents for the container. Since we may choose the most suitable of these senses of the word, why should we not think that the belly and entrails of doves are meant here, which, though they are usually thrown away, were in a time of most severe famine not only kept, but even sold off and disposed of at a great price?" This is Fuller's opinion, in which (if I may say so with all respect to a most careful writer) I seem to find not a few things that have not even the appearance of truth. Thus, that the entrails of doves should be called דביונים in Hebrew has never occurred to anyone even in a dream. Rather, all explain it as excrement, so named from flowing, just as in Greek ῥεῦμα γαστρὸς [rheuma gastros] and διάῤῥοια [diarrhoia], and in Latin alvi profluvium [flux of the belly], are said of this kind of flux. And in Celsus the febres fluentes [flowing fevers], in Greek ῥοώδεις πυρετοὶ [rhoōdeis pyretoi], are those which loosen the bowels. Again, in what the same Fuller asserts, that the word חור means 1. white, 2. a hole, 3. a cavity, 4. the belly, crop, entrails, 5. excrement, most is fabricated. חור for white is not so much Hebrew as Chaldee and Arabic. But for a hole or a cavity it is Hebrew, and from a different root. For the former is from חור chavar, to grow white; the latter from the geminate חרר charar, to perforate. Accordingly you may read in the Talmud, tractate Succa, fol. 20b, חור שחררוהו מים, a hole which water has bored. And for the same Talmudists חריר is the eye of a needle, as ܚܪܘܪܐ is for the Syrians in Matth. XIX, 24. Further, that this חור also means belly, or crop, or entrails, [col. 43] is a mere fabrication, whose author is not cited, nor indeed can be cited, since no one has ever used it so. Finally, חר, or rather חרי, or חרא, for excrement, is an altogether different word, whose root is neither חור nor חרר, but חרה or חרא. Hence the Talmudists consistently write חרי or חריא. And in Arabic خري [kharī] charia, with hamza at the end, means to void excrement, خرء [khurʾ] excrement, مخرأة [makhraʾa] latrine. Indeed the Hebrews too, when they write in full, insert Aleph, as in Esa. XXXVI, 12. לאכול את חראיהם, to eat their own dung. And 2 Reg. X, 27. They destroyed the house of Baal and made it למחראות, into latrines. Nor is the Aleph there adventitious, as they think, but radical, and to be supplied where it is missing, as is clear from Arabic usage. These points observed, it appears that the eminent Fuller did not know the etymology of the word or its true spelling, and indiscriminately took three words of different origin, which led him astray. For since whatever he adduces rests solely [II, 579] on the etymologies of words, if these etymologies are false, whatever is built upon them must also be false. And truly most futile is what he ascribes to the sacred author, that a cab of the bellies and entrails of doves was sold in Samaria for five shekels. For it has never been heard of that the crop and entrails of doves were sold separately. I admit that one reads this of hens, and that in Arabic تبودك [tabūdak] thabudach is the name for one who sells the entrails of a hen, namely the heart, gizzard, etc. Alcamus explains it as من يبيع ما في بطون الدجاج من القلب والقانصة [man yabīʿu mā fī buṭūn al-dajāj min al-qalb wa-l-qāniṣa] But of doves' entrails nothing of the kind occurs anywhere, so far as I know. Nor is it fitting that doves' intestines should have been measured by cabs. For the cab is a measure not of entrails but of grains, like the seah, ephah and cor. Six cabs make a seah, three seahs an ephah, ten ephahs a cor, the largest dry measure. Accordingly in the Talmud and in the Aruch you read everywhere קב חטין, a cab of wheat. And it is defined by Elias as מדת היובש, a measure of dry things; by Pomarius as מרת של חטום, a grain measure; by Aquinas as מדת למדות דבר היבש, a measure for measuring a dry thing. So in Pollux, Κάβασον δὲ ἐκάλουν τὸν περὶ τὴν τροφὴν ἄπληστον, etc. Κάβος γὰρ σίτου μέτρον [Kabason de ekaloun ton peri tēn trophēn aplēston, etc. Kabos gar sitou metron]. They called cabasus one insatiable for food, etc. For the cab is a measure of grain. And in Hesychius, Κάβαισος· ἄπληστος· κάβος γὰρ μέτρον σιτικόν [Kabaisos; aplēstos; kabos gar metron sitikon]; Cabasus, insatiable; for the cab is a grain measure. From this correct Suidas, who has κάβαιστος [kabaistos] for κάβαισος [kabaisos]. And the Etymologicum, which has μετασιτικὸν [metasitikon], a word of no meaning, for μέτρον σιτικὸν [metron sitikon]. But in Hesychius what follows a little below is corrupt, Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ οἰνικὸν [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai oinikon], Cab, a measure of grain and of wine. For that the cab is a measure of wine, or of liquids, you will read nowhere else. So I emend thus: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ κάδος οἰνικόν [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai kados oinikon]; The cab is a measure of grain, and the cadus of wine. He compares two words close in sound as well as in meaning. For both mean a measure, but the latter of wine, the former of grain. Indeed, that the cadus is a measure of wine, as the cab is of grain, there is no one who does not know.
